RECOGNITION AND NISARGADATTA: THE FELT SELF AND THE DIRECT POINTING

"You are that" and the recognition-thesis — the non-dual meeting of the IPVV and the Advaita-advaita sage

2. The convergence, made precise

  • e convergence can be mapped term for term:

  • cease to identify with the body-mind | recognition removes the identification with the finite self-positioning | the false identification is removed, not the self |
  • "be as you are" / the direct pointing | the lover-image: the near turned into the enjoyed (V3P) | the felt return to what was always present |
  • The deep convergence:* both hold that the felt self is primary, that the ultimate is a *return
  • othing added), and that liberation is the removal of a false identification. This is the
  • cognition-thesis, stated in Nisargadatta's modern voice.

  • points to the felt "I am" and stops. The IPVV posits: the ultimate is the one consciousness, the

  • lt "I am" is the pointer; the reality pointed to is not captured by any characterization. This is a
  • fusal to posit the ground — a refusal that aligns him with Ñāṇananda (who refuses the demand for a
  • nal picture behind appearances) against the IPVV (which posits the one).
  • The IPVV's positing.* The IPVV *argues for the one — the transcendental argument of the order-less
  • pport (V2O), the causal proof of the one knower (V2P). It does not merely point; it proves (up to the
  • mmitment). The IPVV's ultimate is not an ineffable pointer but the argued Lord — the felt
  • lf-awareness identified with the parā-vāk, the sphurattā, the māheśvarya.
  • The precise difference.** Nisargadatta: the felt is the pointer to the ineffable; no ground is posited.
  • e IPVV: the felt is the argument for the ground; the Lord is posited and argued. Both start from the
  • lt; they diverge on whether the felt reveals a posited ground (IPVV) or points to an un-posited,

5. Where Nisargadatta joins the honest boundary

6. The synthesis: two voices of one recognition

  • e comparison yields a synthesis. Nisargadatta and the IPVV are two voices of the same recognition:
  • The felt is primary. Both: the felt "I am" / vimarśa is the essence.
  • Recognition adds nothing. Both: the return, the removal of the false identification.
  • The self was never absent. Both: the eternal "I am" / the "I was never not."
  • The direct pointing (Nisargadatta) and the argument (IPVV). The one points; the other proves.
  • The boundary. Nisargadatta refuses to posit the ground; the IPVV posits and argues it (up to the
  • mmitment).
  • The single insight.* Recognition sounds like Nisargadatta because it *is the same insight — the felt
  • -cognition of the self, the removal of the false identification, nothing added. Nisargadatta is the
  • dern, direct, non-systematic voice of the recognition-thesis's felt core. And his refusal to posit the
  • ound is the honest boundary: the felt is shared, the ground is the commitment. Recognition — in
  • sargadatta and in the IPVV — is the felt re-cognition of the self; where it goes beyond the felt (the
  • sited Lord) is the wager.
